item.research_question: How can single-atom platinum catalysts be engineered to become active for methanol oxidation reaction (MOR) when they are typically inert on carbon supports?
item.material_system: Pt single atoms supported on RuO2 (Pt1/RuO2), Pt single atoms on carbon black (Pt1/VXC-72), and control samples including Pt nanoparticles on RuO2 and Pt on metallic Ru
item.processing_route: Simple impregnation-adsorption method: 50 mg RuO2 dispersed in 80 mL distilled water, 0.25 mL of H2PtCl6·6H2O solution (2 mg mL‒1) added dropwise, stirred at 70 °C for 5 h, followed by filtration, washing, and drying at 70 °C overnight
item.test_conditions: Electrochemical tests in N2-saturated 0.1 mol L‒1 KOH and 1 mol L‒1 methanol solution at 25 °C; cyclic voltammetry at 50 mV s−1; chronoamperometry at −0.1 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) for 10 h; CO stripping tests from −0.95 to 0 V at 50 mV s−1
key_findings: Pt1/RuO2 exhibited a mass activity of 6766 mA mg‒1Pt at 0.80 V vs. RHE, which is 15.3 times higher than commercial Pt/C (441 mA mg‒1Pt at 0.92 V vs. RHE)
Pt1/VXC-72 showed no electrocatalytic peak in cyclic voltammetry, confirming it is inactive towards methanol oxidation
The forward-to-backward peak current ratio (If/Ib) for Pt1/RuO2 was 3.67, more than twice that of commercial Pt/C (1.81), indicating superior CO tolerance
After 10 h stability testing, Pt1/RuO2 retained 95.5% of its activity (degradation of 4.5%), whereas commercial Pt/C degraded by ~22%
Annealing Pt1/RuO2 at 700 °C caused Pt aggregation into 30 nm nanoparticles, resulting in complete loss of MOR activity
Reducing Pt1/RuO2 in H2 to form Pt1/RuO2-H (Pt‒Ru coordination) resulted in no MOR activity, whereas the original Pt‒O coordination was active
DFT calculations predicted an activation barrier of 0.49 eV for the rate-limiting dehydrogenation of CH2O* on Pt1/RuO2, lower than the 0.71 eV for pure RuO2(110)
CO electrooxidation on Pt1/RuO2 occurred at an onset potential of 0.152 V, significantly lower than 0.448 V for commercial Pt/C and 0.276 V for Pt1/VXC-72
item.mechanism: The authors propose that the specific coordination environment of Pt‒O3f (3-fold coordinatively bonded O)‒Rucus (coordinatively unsaturated Ru) with undercoordinated bridging O (Obr) in Pt1/RuO2 favors the electrochemical dehydrogenation of methanol. The empty anti-bonding dz2 orbital of Rucus stabilizes the adsorbate, while the filled anti-bonding dz2 orbital of Pt destabilizes intermediates like formaldehyde, lowering the activation barrier for dehydrogenation. Additionally, the oxophilic RuO2 support facilitates water dissociation to form adsorbed OH, which aids in the oxidative removal of COads at low potentials.
item.limitations: The text states that it is still challenging to engineer single-atom catalysts for electrocatalytic methanol oxidation and that previous studies focused only on Pt active centers while neglecting the surrounding environment. The authors also note that Pt single atoms on carbon are inert and that high-temperature annealing leads to aggregation and loss of activity.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that the discovery of Pt1/RuO2 SACs provides an approach to explore Pt SACs for direct alcohol fuel cells and related alcohol oxidation reactions.
quotes: Pt1/RuO2 has good electrocatalytic activity towards methanol oxidation in an alkaline media with a mass activity that is 15.3-times higher than that of commercial Pt/C

The presence of Pt‒O3f (3-fold coordinatively bonded O)‒Rucus (coordinatively unsaturated Ru) bonds with the undercoordinated bridging O in Pt1/RuO2 favors the electrochemical dehydrogenation of methanol
The Pt1/RuO2 SACs showed superb mass activity (6766 mA mg‒1Pt) and stability towards the MOR, far superior to those of most Pt-based catalysts developed to date

records.text: Paper card. Question: How can single-atom platinum catalysts be engineered to become active for methanol oxidation reaction (MOR) when they are typically inert on carbon supports?. System: Pt single atoms supported on RuO2 (Pt1/RuO2), Pt single atoms on carbon black (Pt1/VXC-72), and control samples including Pt nanoparticles on RuO2 and Pt on metallic Ru. Processing: Simple impregnation-adsorption method: 50 mg RuO2 dispersed in 80 mL distilled water, 0.25 mL of H2PtCl6·6H2O solution (2 mg mL‒1) added dropwise, stirred at 70 °C for 5 h, followed by filtration, washing, and drying at 70 °C overnight. Test conditions: Electrochemical tests in N2-saturated 0.1 mol L‒1 KOH and 1 mol L‒1 methanol solution at 25 °C; cyclic voltammetry at 50 mV s−1; chronoamperometry at −0.1 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) for 10 h; CO stripping tests from −0.95 to 0 V at 50 mV s−1. Findings: Pt1/RuO2 exhibited a mass activity of 6766 mA mg‒1Pt at 0.80 V vs. RHE, which is 15.3 times higher than commercial Pt/C (441 mA mg‒1Pt at 0.92 V vs. RHE); Pt1/VXC-72 showed no electrocatalytic peak in cyclic voltammetry, confirming it is inactive towards methanol oxidation; The forward-to-backward peak current ratio (If/Ib) for Pt1/RuO2 was 3.67, more than twice that of commercial Pt/C (1.81), indicating superior CO tolerance; After 10 h stability testing, Pt1/RuO2 retained 95.5% of its activity (degradation of 4.5%), whereas commercial Pt/C degraded by ~22%; Annealing Pt1/RuO2 at 700 °C caused Pt aggregation into 30 nm nanoparticles, resulting in complete loss of MOR activity; Reducing Pt1/RuO2 in H2 to form Pt1/RuO2-H (Pt‒Ru coordination) resulted in no MOR activity, whereas the original Pt‒O coordination was active; DFT calculations predicted an activation barrier of 0.49 eV for the rate-limiting dehydrogenation of CH2O* on Pt1/RuO2, lower than the 0.71 eV for pure RuO2(110); CO electrooxidation on Pt1/RuO2 occurred at an onset potential of 0.152 V, significantly lower than 0.448 V for commercial Pt/C and 0.276 V for Pt1/VXC-72. Mechanism: The authors propose that the specific coordination environment of Pt‒O3f (3-fold coordinatively bonded O)‒Rucus (coordinatively unsaturated Ru) with undercoordinated bridging O (Obr) in Pt1/RuO2 favors the electrochemical dehydrogenation of methanol. The empty anti-bonding dz2 orbital of Rucus stabilizes the adsorbate, while the filled anti-bonding dz2 orbital of Pt destabilizes intermediates like formaldehyde, lowering the activation barrier for dehydrogenation. Additionally, the oxophilic RuO2 support facilitates water dissociation to form adsorbed OH, which aids in the oxidative removal of COads at low potentials.. Limitations: The text states that it is still challenging to engineer single-atom catalysts for electrocatalytic methanol oxidation and that previous studies focused only on Pt active centers while neglecting the surrounding environment. The authors also note that Pt single atoms on carbon are inert and that high-temperature annealing leads to aggregation and loss of activity.. Future work: The authors suggest that the discovery of Pt1/RuO2 SACs provides an approach to explore Pt SACs for direct alcohol fuel cells and related alcohol oxidation reactions.. Quote: "Pt1/RuO2 has good electrocatalytic activity towards methanol oxidation in an alkaline media with a mass activity that is 15.3-times higher than that of commercial Pt/C"
